newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan said in need of insurance protection scheme.
newsitem.headline: Japan said in need of insurance protection scheme.

text.p: The shutdown of a Japanese life insurer last week has raised fresh concerns about the health of others in the industry and prompted calls for authorities to speed up their work on a proper scheme to deal with any future failures.

The Finance Ministry last Friday ordered Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co to halt all operations except for servicing existing customers, the first time an insurer has been forced to shut down in the postwar period.
The Life Insurance Association of Japan is working on a scheme to wind up Nissan Mutual Life using funds from a 200 billion yen ($1.57 billion) solvency fund.

That fund would cover the 200 billion yen ($1.57 billion) gap by which Nissan Mutual said its liabilities exceeded its assets, but analysts noted that it would prove insufficient should added liabilities be uncovered.

Credit rating agency Standard & Poor's said this week that the closure of Nissan Mutual would "test the adequacy" of the policyholder guarantee fund. But S&P added it was not changing its ratings for other insurers as a result of the shutdown.

Finance Ministry officials, meanwhile, are discussing creating a permanent "safety net" to protect insurance policy holders, a body that analysts said might be modelled on the quasi-governmental Deposit Insurance Corporation for banks.

"There is no definite scheme at present and they can't keep relying solely on other insurance companies," said an analyst with the research arm of a Japanese brokerage. "They might also need to consider the use of public money," he added.

Japanese media have also urged the prompt creation of a framework to ensure benefit payments to policy holders when an insurer fails, as well as improvements in financial disclosure by insurance companies.
"The greatest challenge emerging from the present episode is the establishment of a system to ensure benefit payements...," said one recent editorial.
Long-running worries about the difficult environment facing other insurers, including 12th-ranked Toho Mutual Life Insurance Co, were rekindled by Nissan Mutual's failure.

Toho Mutual said on Friday that its on-going restructuring efforts were having a positive effect and that it would be able to post a current profit again for the fiscal year ended on March 31, 1997. The results will be announced on June 10.

Analysts said a permanent wind-up scheme would be vital should a large insurer suffer Nissan Mutual's fate. "If a large insurer fails and authorities don't have a proper scheme, they won't be able to cope," the Japanese analyst said.
Many insurers suffer from the same bad-loan woes that afflict other financial firms which expanded loan portfolios during Japan's 1980s "bubble" economy of soaring asset prices.
They have also been squeezed by Japan's hyper-easy credit policy, which eroded yields on investments and forced some into risky businesses to cover losses on non-performing loans.

Analysts say large insurers are likely to have enough unrealised profits on shareholdings to cover sudden losses, write-offs and negative spreads between investment yields and promised payouts, but some smaller firms may have little cushion left.

But diagnosing the financial health of insurers, which are not listed on the stock exchange, can be tough given accounting practices which do not require full disclosure of unrealised investment losses, analysts added.
"There are a lot of numbers that can't be seen on the surface," the Japanese analyst said.
